tagline: The front door of IT — fix real problems for real people, and learn the whole stack one ticket at a time.
what_you_do: You diagnose and fix the everyday tech problems a business runs into: locked accounts, laptops that won't boot, printers that won't print, software that won't install. You work over phone, chat, and remote sessions — or deskside — resolving what you can and escalating what you can't, documenting every ticket as you go. It's the most accessible front door into IT precisely because it exposes you to a little of everything: Windows, networking, hardware, accounts, and people. Almost every sysadmin and network admin started here.
day_in_life: Work the ticket queue — password resets, account lockouts, and 'my email stopped working' triage
Remote into a user's laptop to fix a VPN client that won't connect, talking them through it calmly
Reimage a machine for a new hire and walk them through first-day setup
Escalate a recurring network drop to the network team with the evidence you gathered, not just 'it's broken'
Write up the fix in the knowledge base so the next tech resolves it in five minutes instead of forty

salary.growth: -3% projected for the group, but ~50,500 openings a year from turnover — churn is exactly why the door stays open
salary.note: U.S. BLS figure for Computer User Support Specialists (15-1232); a median is the midpoint of everyone employed, so entry pay runs lower. Verify against the live BLS page before deciding.

downsides: A lot of it is repetitive — password resets and the same five problems on loop. Many desks measure you on handle time and tickets closed, which adds pressure. Some users treat support as low-status, and L1 phone work is the tier most exposed to AI chatbots and self-service portals. The fix for all of it is the same: treat help desk as a 1–2 year launchpad, not a destination.

fits_if: You genuinely like helping people and can stay patient when they're frustrated
You want the broadest possible exposure to IT before picking a specialty
You learn best by fixing real problems, not just reading about them
less_ideal_if: Talking to people all day drains you fast
Repetition frustrates you and you can't treat it as reps
You expect to start in security or engineering without a support rung first

skills.name: Windows troubleshooting & administration
skills.note: The OS on most corporate desks — user profiles, updates, drivers, event logs.

skills.name: Customer communication & de-escalation
skills.note: The skill that actually separates good techs — explain clearly, stay calm, never condescend.

skills.name: Account & identity basics (AD, password resets, MFA)
Networking fundamentals (IP, DNS, Wi-Fi, VPN)
skills.note: Knowing why it can't connect — not just rebooting the router — is what gets you promoted.

skills.name: Scripting basics (PowerShell)
skills.note: Automating the repetitive stuff is your escape route from it.

certs.title: Google IT Support Certificate
certs.reason: The cheapest structured way to learn the job from zero — and completers get 30% off the A+ vouchers that come next.

certs.title: Cisco CCST IT Support
certs.reason: One $125 exam versus A+'s two ~$274 vouchers — current content, smaller HR footprint. The honest trade-off is in the guide.

certs.title: CompTIA A+
certs.reason: THE recognized entry signal for support roles — hardware, OS, troubleshooting fundamentals.

certs.title: CompTIA Network+
certs.reason: The natural next rung — proves the networking fundamentals that unlock desktop support and NOC roles.

trial.objective: Do the actual job once: pick a real problem on your own computer, reproduce it, diagnose it methodically, fix it, and write it up like a ticket.
trial.disclosure: Fully local — your own machine, built-in tools only; nothing installed or transmitted.

roadmap.title: Learn the fundamentals
roadmap.focus: Hardware, Windows, and troubleshooting method — free via Professor Messer's A+ series. Practice on your own machine: break things, fix them, write up what you did.

roadmap.title: Prove it and get hired
roadmap.focus: Earn CompTIA A+ to get past resume filters, then apply broadly — help desk, MSPs, school districts, hospitals. The first job matters more than the perfect job.

roadmap.title: Level up on the job
roadmap.focus: Volunteer for the harder tickets, learn the network behind them, and add CompTIA Network+ — the rung that moves you from L1 phones to desktop support and NOC roles.

roadmap.title: Pick your exit ramp
roadmap.focus: After 1–2 years, branch toward systems administration, networking, or security. Help desk is the launchpad — the whole point is to leave it upward.

adjacent_paths.reason: The classic promotion path once you know how the network behind the tickets works.
Deskside experience with users and endpoints feeds directly into systems work.
